correctness.rationale: The width relation follows from the exact height of the regular Euclidean \(r\)-disk triangle. Rotating the radius vector of the continued side arc gives exact formulas for the changed vertex, chord lengths, and Euclidean triangle-area increment. Adding exact minor circular-segment areas yields the stated finite-\(x\) deficit. Direct differentiation gives \(a'(0)=c\), \(b'(0)=(c-\sqrt3u)/2\), \(D'(0)=s(\sqrt3c-u)/4\), and \(J_r'(s)=ru^2/c\), hence the displayed \(L(r,w)\). Its alternative sine form is positive on \(0<u\le1/2\). The lead source states that the deformed body has diameter \(a(x)\), and the general diameter--Hausdorff inequality then forces the explicit stability-constant lower bound. Finite verifier checks are supplementary only.

Its Section 5 bounds the added area from above by a sector term and a segment difference; it does not state the exact area law, exact first derivative, or explicit finite-\(r\) canonical lower bound. The isominwidth precursor and the classical Pál stability paper do not imply the finite-\(r\) coefficient. Searches over equivalent formulations and nearby stability literature found no stronger coverage.

value.rationale: The recent lead paper uses this exact deformation as its canonical witness that linear Hausdorff stability is optimal, but loses all finite-r constant information in an upper-bound argument. The exact deficit and slope quantify the efficiency of that designated extremal path and force an explicit lower bound on every local stability constant. The coefficient naturally links the Reuleaux endpoint to the classical Pál limit, making it a useful calibration target rather than an arbitrary parameter slice.
